title: Promoting Intrinsic Motivation
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership makes the case that leaders should cultivate intrinsic rather than purely extrinsic motivation in their teams. The piece cites decades of research showing intrinsically motivated people overcome adversity and outperform others, then asks why leaders default to rewards and punishments anyway. Its answer is candid: extrinsic motivators are easier and work in the short term, while designing for intrinsic motivation is not obvious. The author grounds the alternative in autonomy, competence and connectedness, and highlights two practical levers: asking team members which work they most enjoy and building it into their roles, and investing in the skills they want to develop. It closes with the claim that people are born with intrinsic motivation and good leaders help them rediscover it.
points: Rewards and punishments shape behavior powerfully but can crowd out people's internal drive to perform.
Leaders lean on extrinsic motivators not because they are better but because they are easier and effective in the short term.
Environments that offer autonomy, investment in competence and enjoyment, and connection to peers raise intrinsic motivation.

Two concrete levers stand out: asking people what work they relish and ensuring part of their daily challenge includes it, and investing in the skills they want to build through clinics, practice and outside experts.
quotes: Research for more than 50 years has proven an important point: Leaders who encourage and promote more intrinsic motivations for those they lead can have a profound impact on what can be accomplished. Those motivated intrinsically overcome adversity and generally outperform others.

In short, because other methods are easier, and they work. Extrinsic motivators such as incentives, increased influence, elevated status, and praise are highly effective, especially in the short term. Moreover, designing ways to promote intrinsic motivation is not always obvious or simple.

So, let’s start with the fundamentals. Any environment where leaders give team members more autonomy, invest in their competence and enjoyment, and create an avenue for connectedness to peers creates higher levels of intrinsic motivation.

Asking team members what tasks, projects, or work they most enjoy and relish is a shortcut to getting them engaged with those assignments. At least a portion of the everyday challenge for team members needs to include work they take pleasure in.

Next, investing in the skills of team members through clinics, practice sessions, and outside experts is yet another avenue to promote intrinsic motivation. Once again, knowing what skills team members want to enhance and giving them the time, resources, and expertise to do so is a big intrinsic winner.
People are born with intrinsic motivation. The best leaders just remind them how to rediscover that inner drive.
